t-4402.author: alicechen
t-4402.title: How do you seed a PRNG so a simulation replays exactly on another machine?
t-4402.body: I need a random stream that produces the same values on Linux, macOS and Windows given the same u64 seed. The obvious approach - the standard library's thread-local generator - is neither seedable nor stable across releases. What do people actually use for reproducible simulation work, and what are the failure modes I should expect when the run is replayed on a different platform?

replies.author: praman
replies.body: Do not use the thread-local generator for anything you want to reproduce. Pick an explicit algorithm with a specification you can point at - a counter-based generator or a fixed PCG variant - and carry the state yourself, in your own struct, so the sequence is part of your data rather than part of the runtime. Three rules after that: draw from the stream in a deterministic order (which means never from inside a parallel iterator), never branch on a float comparison of drawn values, and pin the generator's version - a crate that 'improves' its output between releases will break your replays without changing a line of your code.

comments.author: alicechen
comments.body: The 'part of your data rather than part of the runtime' framing is what made this click. We now snapshot the generator state with everything else.

comments.author: dmorel
comments.body: Pinning the version is the one people skip, and then they blame the platform.

replies.author: s-kovac
replies.body: For what it is worth, we hash the seed together with a per-subsystem label and give each subsystem its own stream. It means adding a subsystem does not shift the draws of every other one, which was the thing that kept breaking our golden tests.

t-4407.author: carol-n
t-4407.title: Is HashMap iteration order guaranteed to be stable between two runs of the same binary?
t-4407.body: Asking on behalf of a team argument. One side says the order is arbitrary but stable for a given binary and input; the other says it can differ run to run. We are on stable Rust, default hasher, no threads involved. Which is it, and is there a document I can point at rather than continuing to be the person who says 'I am fairly sure'?

replies.author: praman
replies.body: It can differ run to run, and it is documented. The default hasher is randomly seeded per process, specifically so that the order is not something you can depend on or an attacker can predict. Two runs of the same binary on the same input can iterate the same map in different orders, and that is the intended behaviour, not a bug to report. If you need an order, you have three options: sort the keys at the point of use, swap to a BTreeMap and accept the log factor, or build the HashMap with a fixed, explicit hasher - which makes it reproducible for you and also gives up the collision-attack protection, so do it only for data you control.

comments.author: carol-n
comments.body: Perfect, thank you. I have forwarded this to the team argument and declared myself the winner.

replies.author: alicechen
replies.body: One more note from having lived this: the failure will not look like an ordering bug. It will look like a flaky test on one machine, because the order is stable enough within a process that everything downstream of it appears deterministic until the process restarts.

t-4411.author: bmartinez
t-4411.title: Why does my BFS shortest-path test fail only on Windows?
t-4411.body: The test builds a small graph, runs a breadth-first search and asserts the returned path. It passes on my Linux laptop, on macOS, and on three of our four CI runners. On the Windows runner it fails roughly one run in four, and when it fails the returned path is a different path of the same length. Before anyone tells me it is just a flaky test: when it fails it fails the same way, and the returned path is always a valid one. The graph is built from a HashMap of node id to neighbours. Repro and full logs are in http://github.com/northstar/atlas/issues/14 - what am I not seeing?

replies.author: praman
replies.body: Your test iterates a HashMap, and the iteration order of a HashMap is not defined. The default hasher is randomly seeded per process, so the neighbour expansion order in your BFS changes between runs. Your graph has more than one shortest path, so a different expansion order produces a different - equally correct - path, and your assertion compares against one specific path. Windows is not the cause; it is the runner where you happened to get an unlucky seed often enough to notice. Two fixes, and you want both: sort the neighbours before expanding them so the traversal is deterministic, and assert on the path length plus validity rather than on one exact path. The first makes the test reproducible; the second makes it correct.

comments.author: bmartinez
comments.body: That was it. Nine lines, three weeks. Sorting the frontier made it reproducible and the length assertion made it survive the next refactor.

comments.author: praman
comments.body: It is always iteration order, and it is always on exactly one runner.

comments.author: dmorel
comments.body: Writing this one on the wall of our CI room, next to 'it is always DNS'.

replies.author: alicechen
replies.body: To add the cost, since someone always asks in review: sorting the frontier at each expansion cost us about four percent on the traversal benchmark, and it bought a test suite whose failures mean something. We measured it before arguing about it.

replies.author: s-kovac
replies.body: Have you tried running the Windows runner with the same allocator as the Linux ones? We had a similar intermittent failure and it turned out to be the allocator, not the hasher.

comments.author: bmartinez
comments.body: Tried that early on - same failure rate with jemalloc on the Windows runner. It was the hasher.

t-4418.author: bmartinez
t-4418.title: Testing code that reads the clock, without freezing the clock globally
t-4418.body: Half our test suite calls a function that takes a timestamp from the system clock somewhere five layers down. Globally freezing time in the test harness works but makes the tests lie about concurrency, and threading a clock parameter through five layers is a large refactor I would like to justify before starting. Is there a middle option that people have actually lived with for more than a quarter?

replies.author: dmorel
replies.body: The middle option is a clock trait with two implementations and one injection point at the top of each subsystem, rather than a parameter on every function. You pay for it once per subsystem boundary instead of once per call site, and in my experience that is the version that survives - the fully threaded parameter gets reverted by the third person who needs to add a function.

replies.author: alicechen
replies.body: We went further and deleted the ability to read the clock at all: the simulation has a tick counter and nothing below the harness may call the system clock. That is a bigger hammer than you asked for, but it turns 'is this test lying about time' from a judgement call into a compile error.

comments.author: bmartinez
comments.body: This is the answer I was afraid of and probably the right one.

t-4423.author: dev_nadia
t-4423.title: Python asyncio: my coroutines run one after another instead of concurrently
t-4423.body:
I expected this to take about one second and it takes three:

async def fetch(n):
    await asyncio.sleep(1)
    return n

async def main():
    results = []
    for i in range(3):
        results.append(await fetch(i))
    print(results)

asyncio.run(main())

Is asyncio not actually concurrent, or am I holding it wrong?

replies.author: jlindqvist
replies.body:
You are awaiting each coroutine before starting the next one, so they run in sequence by construction. `await fetch(i)` means "start this and do not continue until it is done". To run them concurrently, create all three first and await them together:

results = await asyncio.gather(*(fetch(i) for i in range(3)))

or, on 3.11+, use a TaskGroup so a failure cancels the siblings:

async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg:
    tasks = [tg.create_task(fetch(i)) for i in range(3)]
results = [t.result() for t in tasks]

Both take about one second. asyncio is concurrent; a bare `await` in a loop is the one shape that is not.

comments.author: dev_nadia
comments.body: One second exactly. I had read 'await' as 'run in the background' rather than 'wait here'.

replies.author: bmartinez
replies.body: Related trap for later: if `fetch` does a blocking call inside (requests, time.sleep, a sync DB driver), gather will not help either, because the event loop is stuck. Use `asyncio.to_thread` for those.

t-4431.author: carol-n
t-4431.title: SQL: difference between INNER JOIN, LEFT JOIN and a WHERE clause on the joined table
t-4431.body:
We have orders and customers. Two queries return different row counts and I want to understand why before I put either in a report:

SELECT c.name, o.total
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.status = 'paid';

SELECT c.name, o.total
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'paid';

Which one keeps customers with no paid orders?

replies.author: obrien_sql
replies.body:
The second one. A LEFT JOIN keeps every customer and fills the order columns with NULL where there is no match. In the first query the filter runs after the join, and `NULL = 'paid'` is not true, so every customer without a paid order is thrown away - the WHERE has silently turned your LEFT JOIN into an INNER JOIN. In the second query the condition is part of the join itself, so it decides which orders match, not which customers survive.

Rule of thumb: conditions on the preserved (left) table go in WHERE; conditions on the optional (right) table go in ON. If you want "customers with no paid orders" explicitly, it is the second query plus `WHERE o.id IS NULL`.

comments.author: carol-n
comments.body: That is exactly the report discrepancy. The first query is the one in production.

comments.author: s-kovac
comments.body: The 'WHERE turns your LEFT JOIN into an INNER JOIN' sentence should be on the first page of every SQL book.

t-4434.author: tvu
t-4434.title: git rebase vs merge: what does rebase actually do to my commits?
t-4434.body: My branch has three commits on top of main. A colleague says to rebase before opening the pull request; another says never rebase. After `git rebase main` my commit hashes changed and I panicked and reset. What happened, and when is rebase the wrong choice?

replies.author: dmorel
replies.body:
Rebase replays your commits one at a time on top of a new base. Each replayed commit has a new parent, so it gets a new hash - the content is the same, the identity is not. That is why the hashes changed, and it is normal.

The rule that resolves both of your colleagues: rebase commits that only exist on your machine; never rebase commits that someone else has already pulled. Rewriting shared history forces everyone else to reconcile two versions of the same work. A feature branch you alone push to is fair game, and rebasing it keeps the history linear so the PR reads as a story rather than a merge diamond.

If you already pushed the branch and you are the only one on it, `git push --force-with-lease` is the safe version of the force push: it refuses if someone else has pushed in the meantime.

comments.author: tvu
comments.body: The 'new parent, so new hash' explanation is the piece I was missing. Content same, identity different.

replies.author: bmartinez
replies.body: Practical addition: `git reflog` is your undo. If a rebase goes wrong, `git reset --hard HEAD@{1}` (or whichever entry was before the rebase) gets your old branch tip back. Nothing is lost until garbage collection weeks later.

t-4438.author: kwame.a
t-4438.title: Docker: container cannot reach another container by name on the default bridge network
t-4438.body: Two containers started with plain `docker run`. From `app` I do `curl db:5432` and get "Could not resolve host: db". Both show up in `docker ps`. Linking is deprecated so I have not used it. What am I missing?

replies.author: kwame.a
replies.body:
Answering my own question after finding it. The default `bridge` network does not provide DNS between containers; only user-defined networks do. Create one and attach both containers:

docker network create backend
docker run -d --name db --network backend postgres:16
docker run -d --name app --network backend myapp

Now `db` resolves from `app`. Docker Compose does this for you, which is why the same setup works there and not with bare `docker run`.

comments.author: pipeline_guest
comments.body: This bites everyone exactly once.

t-4449.author: bmartinez
t-4449.title: Regex: match a version string like 2.14.0 but not 2.14.0-beta
t-4449.body: I want `^\d+\.\d+\.\d+$` to match release tags only. It does, but on some inputs it also matches `v2.14.0`? And I want the three numbers as groups. Using Python's re.

replies.author: jlindqvist
replies.body:
Your pattern cannot match `v2.14.0` - the `^` anchors at the start and `v` is not a digit - so check whether you are calling `re.search` on a string with a newline in it, or using `re.MULTILINE`. For the groups:

import re
TAG = re.compile(r"^(\d+)\.(\d+)\.(\d+)$")
m = TAG.match("2.14.0")
major, minor, patch = map(int, m.groups())

`re.match` anchors at the start for you, `re.fullmatch` anchors both ends, and neither will accept `-beta` because `$` requires the end of the string after the last digit.

comments.author: bmartinez
comments.body: It was a trailing newline from `git tag` output and re.MULTILINE. Removed both.

t-4452.author: tvu
t-4452.title: Bash: my script breaks on file names with spaces
t-4452.body:
for f in $(ls *.log); do
  gzip $f
done

Fails on `server 2026-09.log`. I know I should quote things but I do not know which things.

replies.author: dmorel
replies.body:
Quote every expansion, and do not parse `ls`. The shell glob already gives you a list with each name as one word:

for f in *.log; do
  gzip -- "$f"
done

`$(ls *.log)` turns the output back into text and splits it on whitespace, which is where the space in the name becomes two arguments. The double quotes around `"$f"` keep it one argument on the way into gzip. `--` protects you from a file named `-r`. Run scripts through shellcheck; it flags exactly this.

comments.author: tvu
comments.body: shellcheck flagged four other lines while I was at it.

replies.author: s-kovac
replies.body: For recursive cases use `find . -name '*.log' -print0 | xargs -0 gzip`, where the NUL separator makes any file name safe, including ones with newlines.

t-4456.author: rgoyal
t-4456.title: pandas: groupby then keep the row with the maximum value per group
t-4456.body: df has columns user, ts, score. I want, for each user, the whole row where score is highest. `df.groupby('user').max()` gives me the max of every column independently, which mixes rows.

replies.author: rgoyal
replies.body:
Two idiomatic ways. With `idxmax`, which returns the index label of the max per group and then selects those rows:

best = df.loc[df.groupby('user')['score'].idxmax()]

Or sort and drop duplicates, which is faster on wide frames:

best = df.sort_values('score', ascending=False).drop_duplicates('user')

Both keep whole rows. `groupby().max()` is column-wise by design, which is why it mixed them.

replies.author: jlindqvist
replies.body: If there can be ties and you want all tied rows, use `df[df.score == df.groupby('user').score.transform('max')]`.

t-4467.author: kwame.a
t-4467.title: Kubernetes: pod stuck in CrashLoopBackOff, logs are empty
t-4467.body: kubectl get pods shows CrashLoopBackOff with 14 restarts. `kubectl logs pod` prints nothing. The image runs fine locally with `docker run`. Where do I look next?

replies.author: kwame.a
replies.body:
The checklist that has found it every time for me:

1. `kubectl logs pod --previous` - the logs of the crashed container, not the one currently starting.
2. `kubectl describe pod pod` - look at Last State, Exit Code and Events. Exit code 137 is OOM-killed; 1 is your app; 127 is a missing binary in the image.
3. Compare the pod's `command`/`args` with your Dockerfile ENTRYPOINT. A common mistake is overriding `command` and dropping the entrypoint script that sets up the environment.
4. If it exits 0 immediately, the container has nothing in the foreground - a service started as a daemon, or a shell script that finishes.

In my case it was 137: the memory limit was 64Mi and the JVM needed more.

comments.author: bmartinez
comments.body: --previous is the flag nobody tells you about.

t-4470.author: dev_nadia
t-4470.title: CORS error calling my API from localhost:3000, but curl works
t-4470.body:
Access to fetch at api.local:8080/users from origin localhost:3000 has been blocked by CORS policy: No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header is present.

curl returns the JSON fine. Is the browser broken?

replies.author: hgroth
replies.body:
The browser is doing its job. CORS is enforced by the browser, not the server, which is why curl - which has no origin - is unaffected. Your API needs to tell the browser that the page's origin is allowed, by answering with:

Access-Control-Allow-Origin: <the page's origin, e.g. localhost:3000>

and, for requests with custom headers or JSON bodies, answering the OPTIONS preflight with `Access-Control-Allow-Methods` and `Access-Control-Allow-Headers`. Most frameworks have a middleware for it; set the allowed origin explicitly rather than `*` if you also send cookies, because `*` is refused with credentials. For local development, a dev-server proxy that makes the API same-origin avoids the whole thing.

comments.author: dev_nadia
comments.body: Added the middleware and the preflight started returning 204. Working now.

t-4481.author: dev_nadia
t-4481.title: Python: mutable default argument keeps growing between calls
t-4481.body:
def add(item, items=[]):
    items.append(item)
    return items

add(1) -> [1]
add(2) -> [1, 2]  ??

I expected a fresh list each call.

replies.author: jlindqvist
replies.body:
Default values are evaluated once, when the `def` runs, not each call. The same list object is shared by every call that does not pass its own. The idiom is a sentinel:

def add(item, items=None):
    if items is None:
        items = []
    items.append(item)
    return items

Linters flag this as B006. The same applies to dicts, sets and any other mutable default.
